p.x:
Every school holiday, I go to my grandpa's farm in Nakhon Ratchasima. It's near a small village, and there are fields everywhere. My grandpa grows rice and vegetables, and he has many animals.
In the morning, I help him feed the chickens and collect their eggs. Then we give food to the pigs and the ducks. Grandpa has two cows, and my grandma makes delicious milk drinks. He also has some goats, but no sheep.
In the past, Grandpa used a buffalo to work in the fields. Now he has a small tractor. The soil on his farm is very good. My job is to pull out the weeds and plant seeds in the garden. In the evening, we sit near the barn and look at the stars. I love the farm because it's quiet and the air is fresh.

p.t: A Year in the Rice Fields
p.x:
Rice is the most important crop in Thailand, and life in many rural areas follows the rice year.
In May or June, when the rainy season begins, farmers plough their fields. In the past they used buffaloes, but today most use machines. Then they sow the rice seeds, or plant young rice plants by hand in the paddy fields, which are covered with water. Rainfall is very important; in a dry year, farmers depend on irrigation from rivers and canals.
During the growing season, farmers must protect the rice from insects and disease. Many use fertiliser and pesticides, but some are now choosing organic methods because chemicals can be expensive and harmful.
The harvest usually takes place in November or December. Families and neighbours often work together to cut the rice. After the harvest, some farmers grow other vegetables or keep livestock such as cows and chickens. Others work in orchards, growing fruit like mangoes and longans.

Agriculture faces a difficult challenge: by 2050, farmers will need to feed nearly ten billion people, using less water and less arable land, in a climate that is becoming less predictable.
In many developing countries, most farmers are smallholders, cultivating just a few hectares. Some still practise subsistence farming, growing only enough to feed their families. For them, the main problems are low incomes and vulnerability to bad weather. One successful solution has been the cooperative, in which farmers combine resources to buy equipment and negotiate better prices.
In richer countries, mechanisation transformed farming during the twentieth century. Tractors and harvesters allowed a single farmer to manage huge areas, and new seeds and chemicals dramatically increased yields. However, this model has costs. Large farms often rely on monoculture, growing the same crop year after year, which exhausts the soil and encourages pests. Traditional methods such as crop rotation, in which different crops are grown in turn, are now being rediscovered.
Technology may offer further answers. Genetically modified crops can resist drought or disease, although many consumers remain suspicious of them. Meanwhile, sensors and drones allow farmers to give each plant exactly the water it needs. Some experts argue that the goal should not be for every country to be self-sufficient, but for the global food system as a whole to become more resilient.
